chunks: 55 - Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Muhammad ibn Isa al-A'badi said:

Abu 'Umar al-Hadda' wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) and I read the letter and the reply in his own handwriting: He informs him that he used to go to some of the judges of these people, and that he had assigned to them endowments and inheritances of some of the children of al-Abbas, both living and dead, and he had provided them with provisions, and indeed he used to fulfill the trust to them. Then after that he made a covenant with Allah that he would not enter into business with them, and there would be expenses on him, and most of what was in his hand has been lost. And I fear that what he does not like to be revealed about the situation will be revealed to them, for he is awaiting your command in that, so what you command him to do.
So he (peace be upon him) wrote to him: 'There is no harm on you if you enter into business with them; Allah knows and we are as you are upon it.'

key_terms.الْحَذَّاءُ: Al-Hadda', a title or name of the narrator Abu 'Umar

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on doing business with the judges of the Umayyads according to Imam al-Rida?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the pragmatic Shia approach to economic transactions with non-Shia authorities during periods of political tension, specifically addressing the permissibility of handling endowments (*waqf*) and inheritances for Abbasid judges. The Imam’s concise reply, 'There is no harm in you entering with them,' emphasizes that the mere association or transaction does not invalidate one's faith or financial standing, provided the core elements of the deal are sound. This ruling alleviates the concern of *ghishsh* (deception or hidden flaw) in the eyes of the Imam, highlighting a flexible jurisprudence that prioritizes practical livelihood over rigid political exclusion.
